title: Graduate underemployment: a detour not a dead end
summary:
This blog was kindly authored by Gina Nkwah, Engagement and Delivery Officer at the NHS Alliance and University of Bath graduate. My peers and I grew up believing that developing high-quality skills through higher education would be the ultimate investment in strong professional opportunities. The post Graduate underemployment: a detour not a dead end appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Gina Nkwah, Engagement and Delivery Officer at the NHS Alliance and University of Bath graduate.

My peers and I grew up believing that developing high-quality skills through higher education would be the ultimate investment in strong professional opportunities. Yet at some point post-graduation, many of us have had to work in economically precarious positions that do not demand graduate-level competencies. This is termed ‘underemployment’.

Underemployment can be common in any well-prepared graduate’s career trajectory. For one, there are more graduates than graduate jobs each year, resulting in a limited supply of roles that integrate graduate-level skills. Higher Education Statistics Agency’s 2023/24 data finds that 25% of UK graduates working in the UK weren’t in high-skilled employment within 15 months of leaving higher education, with higher figures for graduates holding non-science degrees. In 2024, only 67.9% of working-age graduates were in high-skilled jobs. Nearly one third of UK graduates are currently in roles that do not require the knowledge and skills gained from a degree, compared to Italy, Germany and Scandinavian countries, where less than a fifth of graduates are underemployed.

Artificial intelligence (AI) screening and rising costs for employers heighten the difficultes applicants face in securing graduate-level roles. When AI systems automatically reject applications based on arbitrary keywords, and employers lack the resources to train new talent, graduates inevitably suffer. As vacancies disappear and rejections abound, graduates are undeniably at a crossroads. Rather than risk long gaps in CVs and dwindling finances, some will eventually settle into less competitive roles which don’t require graduate-level skills.

Multi-year graduate underemployment risks undermining specialist skills developed through university study and hinders lifetime earning trajectories. If an underemployed graduate later applies for higher-skilled roles, a lack of graduate-level work experience on their CV can lead to fewer successful applications. A paper published by the IZA Institute of Labor Economics terms this phenomenon the ‘scarring effect’ and finds that persistent underemployment for 6 months results in an increased probability of later underemployment. This may affect a graduate’s ability to repay student loans, enter the housing market and comfortably participate in other aspects of civic and personal life.

Early underemployment is particularly detrimental for women, Black people, people in low higher education participation areas, and other underprivileged demographics. Research from the IZA Institute of Labor Economics finds that these groups have a higher probability of underemployment at 42 months post-graduation. The scarring effect of underemployment, coupled with pre-existing inequalities faced by these groups, produces a severe impact on labour market outcomes and hinders potential talent.

Critically, reducing graduate underemployment is in everyone’s interest. A graduate’s participation in the labour market, in a role matched to their skills, leads to greater job satisfaction, higher lifetime earnings and faster loan repayments. These outcomes can secure positive individual outcomes while preventing long-term costs to the public purse. Likewise, for higher education institutions, strong graduate employment statistics bolster their competitive edge and student uptake. Better economic outcomes can also impact the likelihood of a graduate pursuing postgraduate education. A 2026 survey of Prospect users, the UK’s biggest graduate careers platform, found that the top concerns about continuing further study were the cost of tuition and the cost of living. Ensuring graduates are in an optimal economic position can support the desire to upskill, essential not just for the sustainability of the higher education sector, but to drive academic exploration irreplaceable by AI.

Practically, how can higher education institutions address and reduce graduate underemployment? Some universities have dedicated professional and pastoral support for study abroad and industry placements. Continual high-quality placement support across all providers strengthens a student’s work ethic, which can increase the likelihood of post-graduation work offers. Where suitable, further collaborations with employers are necessary to address early training concerns as a barrier to hiring young talent. Universities UK finds that 52% of employers said graduates require more development than they had anticipated, which likely occurs when workplaces lack necessary resources to train graduates. New ways of approaching student placements, such as through integrating ‘Learning in the Workplace’ assessments to develop workplace skills, can allow students dedicated time to integrate academic theory into their activities within their placement. These collaborations provide students a stronger foundation to weather a market with limited finances for training graduates.

Higher education institutions are pivotal in strengthening a student’s adaptability and resilience within a technology-mediated recruitment landscape. Students want to see clear career guidance on where human skills remain essential. Universities and colleges can provide hands-on and virtual training or courses to identify how to champion human skills within applications in ways that highlight their long-term value in the workplace. Universities UK’s Future Jobs Roadmap further outlines recommendations to accelerate graduate employability and meet rapidly changing skills needs.

Ultimately, a variety of labour market pressures can make underemployment an inevitable journey in a graduate’s life. The higher education sector is crucial in boosting a student’s fortitude amidst the road bumps, ensuring that underemployment is not a graduate’s career totality.

title: We are teaching children maths they will never use. Isn’t it better to help them speak fluently? | Simon Jenkins
summary:
The education secretary is right to focus on what students need most: the ability to express themselves. As for maths, grab a calculator

At last the fourth R is born. Articulation – speaking – is to join reading, writing and arithmetic in the education canon. What has become the mighty struggle against the dictatorship of the screen can begin in earnest. The spoken word, human-to-human communication, must finally be recognised by the gods of reactionary schooling. The pundits call it oracy.

On Thursday, the education secretary, Lucy Powell, called the academics’ bluff. She wants a radical reform of the national curriculum in England to reduce “desktop” working in favour of verbal fluency and practical skills. This will take courage. For decades, education’s senior leaders have been ramming easily forgotten “subjects”, such as maths and French, into children’s brains so they can be judged and measured in league tables. These tables have grown ever more dominant as ministers seek to climb “global rankings”.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

Continue reading...
full_text:
At last the fourth R is born. Articulation – speaking – is to join reading, writing and arithmetic in the education canon. What has become the mighty struggle against the dictatorship of the screen can begin in earnest. The spoken word, human-to-human communication, must finally be recognised by the gods of reactionary schooling. The pundits call it oracy.

On Thursday, the education secretary, Lucy Powell, called the academics’ bluff. She wants a radical reform of the national curriculum in England to reduce “desktop” working in favour of verbal fluency and practical skills. This will take courage. For decades, education’s senior leaders have been ramming easily forgotten “subjects”, such as maths and French, into children’s brains so they can be judged and measured in league tables. These tables have grown ever more dominant as ministers seek to climb “global rankings”.

After the second world war, an “academic” secondary education was shaped by the increased demand for a university-educated workforce. Higher education was expanded, but Britain’s technical and vocational schools and colleges were relegated out of sight. Teaching became enslaved to exam quantification and lost contact with the real world.

But the act of excluding communication skills from this academic orthodoxy has come home to roost. Artificial intelligence and mobile phones are progressively distancing young people from adults and each other. I notice gatherings of young people who used to chatter, laugh and banter. They now stand gazing at their screens or they just shout at each other. Conversation – sharing, informing, discussing, sympathising – seems on the way out.

Speaking itself is going out of fashion. Research suggests that in the past two decades the number of words people say each day has shrunk by nearly a third. They prefer texting. A quarter of young people now say they never even answer the phone unless pre-arranged. They fear a phone call means bad news.

Powell’s promotion of oracy means teaching young people once again to use the spoken word to their advantage. It is about conveying what one means clearly; listening, debating and handling disagreement. Speaking well means using eye contact and appropriately adjusting your tone of voice. It means politeness and tolerance. Above all, it enables young people to present themselves to others effectively, whether in work, play, argument or friendship.

To the Greeks and Romans, oracy was the towering skill of rhetoric. It was central to citizenship. The New Education movement of Steiner and Montessori in early 20th-century Europe stressed building on the qualities of the individual child rather than imposing rote learning from above. It is significant that the movement has seen a revival in the Waldorf schools now favoured by California’s AI executives in Silicon Valley.

That such ideals of progressive education have long been drummed out of the English curriculum is outrageous. The aversion to the spoken word has corresponded with the increasing prominence of maths in the curriculum, its skills beyond foundational arithmetic irrelevant to all but a tiny minority of adults. Children need to master elementary maths in primary school. But after that they only need to know how to use a calculator. I wonder how many readers remember being able to answer this question from last year’s GCSE paper: “The volume of a sphere is 4/3πr³ where r is the radius. Work out the volume of a sphere with diameter 20cm in terms of π.”

It is extraordinary that passing this exam is still required for most apprenticeships. Yet while he was prime minister, Rishi Sunak wanted maths to be compulsory until the age of 18. Small wonder it has long headed the list of “most hated” school subjects.

Quite how the teaching profession will react to Powell is not clear. The hyper-centralisation of British government has meant ever more school time spent on exams. This has led to cutting back on individualised learning and creativity, which typically flourishes in teaching of the arts. Teachers are pressed to “teach to the test”, at peril of damnation from Ofsted. These days, only the private sector dares resist. Winchester college devotes an hour a day to its form of oracy: “div” and “forum” sessions, when pupils discuss contemporary topics not covered by the examination syllabus: scientific ideas, philosophy, politics, music, critical thinking and the acceptance of others’ opinions.

Such speech-centred concepts as group learning and peer tutoring are being pursued in some universities, and the cause was taken forward in the 2024 oracy commission report. But the catch is always resources. The essence of teaching people how to speak must lie in personal contact. It is in the human relationship of tutor and pupil, which was once the essence of teaching as a profession, not a mechanical skill.

One key might lie in killing maths. Leave it to its enthusiasts. For the rest, school should be about the world outside, a world of other human beings. It is about how to go about handling them that young people have most to learn.

title: A Planned Intellectual Diversity Accreditation Standard Draws Opposition
summary:
A Planned Intellectual Diversity Accreditation Standard Draws Opposition
Ryan Quinn Fri, 10/16/2026 - 03:00 AM

The American Association of University Professors president told the Commission on Colleges and Universities that institutions shouldn’t “be expected to prioritize intellectual pluralism on settled scholarly questions.”

Byline(s)
Ryan Quinn
full_text:
The American Association of University Professors is opposing a higher education accreditor’s plan to begin evaluating institutions on “intellectual pluralism” and “intellectual diversity”—a term the AAUP notes is connected to conservative criticism of colleges and universities and to the Trump administration’s continued push to transform them.

The pushback against the Commission on Colleges and Universities (formerly known as the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges, or SACSCOC) underscores the difficulties that long-standing accreditation agencies like it face as Trump seeks to overhaul this niche, but fundamental, aspect of the relationship between the federal government and higher ed. The commission is one of the largest accreditors in the country, overseeing more than 780 colleges and universities. But it’s faced push back from Republican lawmakers in recent years who felt the accreditor was overstepping its role.

For a university, earning accreditation unlocks access to federal student aid, including student loan money—but only if the accreditor recognizing the institution is itself recognized by the Education Department. Under Trump, that department is pressuring existing accreditors to assess institutions using some undefined criteria, such as intellectual diversity, while simultaneously promoting new accreditors to compete with them.

Last month, the commission released a new draft of its Principles of Accreditation, the standards universities will be expected to meet to earn and maintain the commission’s imprimatur.

Among the commission’s roughly 30 proposed standards is a new one, titled “Intellectual Pluralism.” If the commission enacts this standard, it will begin assessing whether colleges publish “policies designed to support, promote, and prioritize intellectual diversity and affirm the respectful, civil exchange of ideas and viewpoints,” and whether those institutions measure “student and faculty perceptions on the range of viewpoints and perspectives offered by the institution or program.”

The draft standard doesn’t define intellectual pluralism or intellectual diversity, or further explain how the commission would assess whether policies are sufficient in this area. The accreditor emailed a general statement but didn’t provide Inside Higher Ed interviews Thursday or answer multiple written questions.

Todd Wolfson, president of the AAUP—which is both a left-leaning faculty union and an over-century-old professional association that wrote landmark definitions of academic freedom and tenure—told the commission in a letter this week that his group is “deeply troubled” by the new standard.

“Institutions of higher education should not be expected to prioritize intellectual pluralism on settled scholarly questions,” Wolfson wrote, “even if certain interests would prefer that their favored opinions be more widely represented on campus.”

Wolfson wrote that conservative writer David Horowitz—who authored The Professors: The 101 Most Dangerous Academics in America—“developed” the term intellectual diversity in 2003. Wolfson also said it appeared the commission proposed this new standard in response to an April 2025 executive order, in which President Trump ordered his education secretary to ensure accreditation requires prioritizing “intellectual diversity amongst faculty,” and in response to the Education Department’s proposed overhaul of the accreditation rules.

The commission’s website does say the new standard is “fully or in part aligned with Department of Education requirements or [is] recommended by [the Accreditation, Innovation and Modernization rule-making committee] to be included in the Federal standards.” But, as Wolfson noted, “executive orders are not laws, and the AIM Committee’s proposed changes have not been adopted.” (The administration is working to finalize the proposed changes, and Trump officials have said they want to do so by Nov. 1. The new rules would then take effect next July.)

Wolfson told Inside Higher Ed that the AAUP doesn’t know of any “other accreditation agency appeasing the Trump administration in this way on ‘intellectual pluralism.’”

In its proposed accreditation rule changes, ED seeks to require accreditors to evaluate whether universities have policies “designed to support, promote, and appropriately prioritize intellectual diversity and the free exchange of ideas amongst faculty, to include elements that address intellectual inquiry and student learning.” Accreditors would also be required to ensure universities measure “student and faculty perceptions on the range of viewpoints and perspectives offered by the institution or program, unless the institution or program has a religious mission,” in which case their policy must include “elements that address intellectual inquiry and student learning” consistent with that mission.

It’s unclear how, or whether, the commission will change its proposed accreditation standard in response to Wolfson’s input. In an emailed statement, commission President Stephen L. Pruitt said the overall “Principles of Accreditation are being revised by a dedicated committee of representatives from our member institutions. This feedback, along with all other feedback we have received, is being presented to the Principles Review Committee for review, discussion, and possible revision.”

The AAUP isn’t the only group that has raised concern about intellectual diversity criteria. In a public comment on ED’s proposal, the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression wrote that while “meaningful exposure to competing ideas, arguments, methods, and schools of thought is an educational good … vague requirements to ‘promote, and appropriately prioritize’ intellectual diversity risk encouraging ideological quotas, compelled curricular balance, viewpoint-based personnel decisions, and ideological auditing.”

Tyler Coward, FIRE’s lead counsel for government affairs and an author of that letter, told Inside Higher Ed the legal analysis isn’t exactly the same when looking at what individual accreditors can do. He said, “The devil will be in the details” when it comes to carrying out what the commission has proposed.

But he said some of the concerns are the same, and if the commission is “citing this [ED] standard that has yet to be adopted as the reason why they’re doing this, perhaps it is premature. This precompliance is a problem, and we see that a lot during the Trump administration.

“There are ways in which this could go from this potentially good idea,” Coward added, to one that means “censoring faculty or creating a chilling effect for certain ideas.”

In an email to Inside Higher Ed, Wolfson listed other concerns AAUP has with the commission’s proposed standards, but also said what the commission is doing with the intellectual pluralism proposal is unique.

“Our biggest concerns are about how loose the language is on academic freedom. It opens the door to potentially bad interpretations,” he added. “They’ve also weakened their standard on shared governance. Genuine shared governance is substantially more than requiring ‘faculty input.’”

title: 4 Ways Colleges Are Rethinking Degree Completion
summary:
4 Ways Colleges Are Rethinking Degree Completion
Joshua.Bay Fri, 10/16/2026 - 03:00 AM

New institutional initiatives and research highlight ways to help transfer students, returning learners and other students navigate college.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Colleges are reconsidering the policies, academic structures and support systems that can make earning a degree unnecessarily difficult, particularly for transfer students, returning adults and those balancing school with other responsibilities.

From expanding bachelor’s degree avenues at two-year colleges to helping stopped-out students return, institutions are exploring new ways to support students through graduation.

Here are four approaches colleges are taking to make degree completion more accessible.

Exploring new transfer pathways between community colleges.

Today, roughly 200 community colleges across 24 states offer bachelor’s degree programs, challenging the notion that community colleges are exclusively two-year institutions.

As such programs expand, they are thrusting community colleges into a new role. While they have traditionally been viewed as starting points for students who transfer to four-year bachelor’s degree–granting institutions, now some community colleges are becoming transfer destinations themselves.

New cross-state partnerships at Yavapai College offer one example. The public community college in Arizona partnered with Moraine Park Technical College in Wisconsin and Central Community College in Nebraska this past spring, creating new avenues for graduates of both institutions to enroll in Yavapai’s bachelor’s degree programs.

Beyond the individual articulation agreements, the model raises broader questions about whether networks of community colleges could share academic capacity, expanding bachelor’s degree opportunities for students without requiring every institution to develop its own four-year programs.

Doug Berry, acting president of Yavapai College, said students can transfer their entire associate degree toward one of Yavapai’s 92-credit bachelor’s degrees, leaving them with roughly 30 to 32 credits to complete. A full-time student could therefore finish a bachelor’s degree with about one additional year of study.

“As a community college, we’re used to having our students complete and then move on to a university,” Berry said. “So when we entered this space, we got a chance to almost reverse-engineer that.”

Allowing students to pursue bachelor’s degrees where they started.

This fall, Generations College, a private, nonprofit two-year institution in Chicago, announced it would offer bachelor’s degrees for the first time in its 122-year history.

Generations’ decision comes as a growing number of two-year colleges nationwide are expanding into four-year degrees, often with the goal of creating more affordable and accessible avenues to a bachelor’s degree.

Grace Alexis, chancellor of Generations College, said the institution will offer four bachelor’s programs: business administration, business administration with an AI focus, entrepreneurship and entrepreneurship with an AI focus. She said the decision to add the degrees was driven in part by students who wanted to continue their education at Generations rather than transfer elsewhere after earning an associate degree.

The bachelor’s programs will require 120 credits, compared with 60 for an associate degree. Students will also have access to the supports Generations already provides, including flexible scheduling, hybrid and online courses, and financial assistance, such as the college’s scholarship program for single parents.

“A lot of them go kicking and screaming. They don’t want to leave because they know that they’re not going to find the experience that they have at Generations at other schools,” Alexis said. “So, because of their many requests to continue their education with us, we felt that we had to remove the barrier.”

Providing more support for students returning to finish their degrees.

Colleges nationwide go to great lengths to re-enroll the millions of Americans who have left higher education with credits but no credential. But bringing students back doesn’t necessarily address the financial, academic and personal challenges that led them to leave in the first place.

A new two-year initiative at the University of Houston–Downtown is testing a more comprehensive approach: It combines personalized advising with emergency financial assistance, community-based basic needs support and efforts to change institutional policies that can make returning to college difficult for working adults.

Backed by $975,000 in philanthropic support, Bridge to Completion aims to create a centralized re-engagement hub for former students who have stopped out since 2018. There, students can receive individualized outreach, degree mapping, academic advising, assistance with readmission and financial aid, career guidance, and personalized plans for returning to college.

Jonathan Davis, interim senior vice president for academic affairs and provost, said the university developed the initiative with the understanding that the stopped-out student population can face an array of challenges as they restart their academic careers. Those can include unpaid institutional balances, transportation and childcare costs, and unexpected expenses.

“Every student’s story is their own, and everyone is a little different, but they kind of rhyme in ways that you notice over time,” Davis said. “By having a coherent effort around these specific populations of high need and high opportunity, then we know we can deploy those resources.”

Pairing academic flexibility with structured support.

Competency-based education offers students an alternative to traditional college courses, allowing them to advance by demonstrating mastery of specific skills and knowledge rather than spending a set amount of time in a classroom. The model is particularly appealing to adult learners, who can progress at a flexible pace and receive credit for knowledge they already possess.

But while flexibility has long been central to competency-based education, new research suggests adult learners don’t necessarily want to be left entirely to their own devices. A national survey of 600 prospective undergraduate and graduate students ages 20 to 59 who planned to enroll or return to school within the next two years found that many want flexibility paired with deadlines, instructor interaction and other structures. The survey was conducted in March and April by MGT and commissioned by DeVry University.

Among prospective graduate students, 86 percent said they could manage their time without strict deadlines, yet 49 percent also said they need deadlines to stay on track and 58 percent preferred structured, instructor-led weekly classes.

The findings also suggest that the availability of CBE could influence some prospective students’ decisions about whether to enroll at all. Some 31 percent of undergraduate prospects and 40 percent of graduate prospects said they would enroll only if a competency-based option were available.

Elise Awwad, president of DeVry University, said the findings highlight a tension between the flexibility prospective students value and the structure they believe they need to succeed.

“The research was eye-opening on the support side, but not eye-opening on the flexibility side,” Awwad said. “It’s not an or, it’s an and. Flexibility matters, but so does having someone there to catch me if I need them.”

title: Pruning
summary:
Pruning
Sara Brady Fri, 10/16/2026 - 03:00 AM

Yes, even small programs incur costs.

Byline(s)
Matt Reed
full_text:
“Why bother cutting that tiny program? It doesn’t affect any jobs. Keeping it doesn’t cost anything!”

If only that were true.

In looking at some programs with very low (or sometimes no) enrollments, I run into this argument regularly. If a given certificate is just a recombination of courses that we teach in other programs already, the argument goes, what’s the harm in keeping it?

The harms are several.

One is the small section problem. When we need to cull small sections to stay within budget, one of the extenuating factors that can save a small section is that someone needs it this semester in order to graduate or complete a program. The more combinations of courses we offer, the more small sections fall into this category. Thin-slicing the same population of students over more options creates more exceptions, each of which brings a cost.

Similarly, a proliferation of options across the curriculum greatly increases overhead in terms of system maintenance, outcomes assessment, program reviews and even just building and keeping the catalog updated. No one certificate does that by itself, but when you have dozens of them, the costs (and confusion) add up.

Speaking of outcomes, I have a substantive concern about producing credentials that have no discernible external value, whether for employment or transfer. Yes, we can manufacture certificates to serve as de facto consolation prizes when someone drops out, but let’s say a student does drop out with one of those and they bring that certificate with them as they look for work. If the real world doesn’t recognize it, what, exactly, have we achieved?

That question is becoming more urgent as the federal administration is talking about withholding financial aid from credentials without discernible market value. If the violations cover more than two years, a college as a whole can lose access to federal student aid. If a few certificates cost us access to Title IV funding, then that’s a catastrophe, and for what?

Locally, we also have a systems issue. Our enterprise resource planning platform, Anthology, allows students to carry only one major at a time. That means that with credentials built on the stackable model: Every time they complete one step, they have to change their major. If they don’t take things in exactly the “correct” order, their financial aid can suffer; aid can only cover courses in the major in which they are registered. Admittedly, that’s a quirk of an unpopular ERP, but we’re stuck with it for now.

That doesn’t mean the pruning process is painless, of course. Students halfway through have a reasonable claim to a teach-out, at least for a while. (If it drags on too long, then you’re right back to the small section problem.) Catalog revisions take some effort. Some people take pruning personally. And there’s the fear of headlines that misunderstand what’s happening and present it in misleading and damaging ways.

In a more perfect world, of course, the stakes would be much lower, and we could treat curricular pruning simply as a matter of tidying up. But in this world, the resources currently spent on bespoke mini-credentials would be better spent shoring up the programs with actual demand. I’d rather do that than pay people for program reviews for programs with almost no students in them.

title: Storytelling, heroes and leadership in higher education today
summary: The post Storytelling, heroes and leadership in higher education today appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Mark Flisher and Rachael Paige explore the potential for storytelling as an ethical approach to leadership development in higher education.

Storytelling as a way to co-construct meaning

It was through informal conversations that we realised there were synergies between our research and professional interests. Mark had spent time exploring embodied experiences of masculinities through Live Art. Rachael’s research was on presence in teaching. Over cups of coffee, we found ourselves wandering through stories, weaving narratives of leading and being led, of how we were guided, facilitated, or sometimes told and moulded. We narrated how the leaders we had encountered had embodied resilience, taken risks, became vulnerable, and how we were surprised that these manifest in our own leadership styles.

Telling stories out loud revealed three significant areas: they helped us understand ourselves and foregrounded our values and belief-systems. They acted as vehicles for meditation, where we could spend time with our leadership actions and align them with our values. They also provided momentum; they helped identify leadership development. We realised that our storytelling could be an ethical leadership-training approach that challenged the image of the ‘Heroic Leader’. This thinking informed a university-wide workshop at the University of Worcester, and this blog.

Challenging the heroic

Reflecting on our experiences, we realised we were questioning the idea that leadership depends on a heroic individual who rescues an organisation through force of personality. We challenged the idea that this ‘superhero’ (Linn, 2011) relies upon an individual’s innate characteristics, dominance, power-based approaches and hierarchical structures.

One story from Rachael’s early teaching career highlighted how strongly those in positions of authority can shape the values and behaviours of less experienced colleagues. We realised that neither of us was entirely comfortable with the idea of the heroic leader. In fact, we had both experienced leadership cultures where confidence, certainty and control were highly valued, sometimes at the expense of trust, collaboration and psychological safety, as a more relational form of leadership would advocate (Fletcher, 2003). We also noticed how these expectations often reflected traditionally masculinised ideas of leadership.

But the more stories we shared, the harder it became to dismiss heroic leadership altogether. We recounted examples of leaders showing courage, resilience and determination in ways that brought people together rather than silencing them. This led us to question whether the real issue was not the behaviour itself, but the intention and context behind it. Perhaps leadership isn’t a simple choice between heroic and relational after all?

What our stories told us

As we reflected on these complexities through our stories, we began to see how our origin stories have shaped some foundational aspects of our leadership: our motivations, values, commitments and priorities.

For Mark, these stories helped him remain accountable to his own principles and to reflect on how those principles were enacted in practice. For Rachael, they provided opportunities for further development.

These moments of critical reflection moved our origin stories into what we have called ‘maturing stories’, highlighting increasingly complex leadership behaviours such as vulnerability, building trust and managing ‘wicked problems’ (Grint, 2005). And encouraged further maturing in recognising we needed to move beyond binary thinking and recognise the value of drawing on the most effective aspects of both heroic and person-centred, relational approaches to leadership.

From ‘I’ to ‘We’

A theme from our conversations emphasised moving language from ‘I’ and ‘you’ towards ‘we’ and ‘us’ (Cunliffe and Erikson, 2011). Relational leadership builds on the idea that leadership does not sit with one individual. It grows through relationships, interactions and the shared experiences that connect people.

We realised that the most effective leaders did not have all the answers but rather built a community of respect, trust, engagement and collaboration. We also recognised that this does not happen by accident. This requires deliberate choices: curiosity over certainty, dialogue over direction, and shared learning over individual authority. In a psychological safe workspace, promoting shared responsibility over blame. Recognising kindness, empathy and openness not as optional soft skills, but as practices that influence culture, strengthen relationships and help people be their best at work.

There is a challenge here for leaders around authentic leadership. For relational leadership to be effective it should be seen to be lived out in the day-to-day. Through our initial exploration of leadership in HE and our sharing of ideas with colleagues, the principle of leadership as not just seen but felt has been important. Therefore, we intend to use these insights to shape our next steps. We want to explore through leader stories how intentions and values are expressed through day-to-day interactions. Ultimately, we hope to use these stories to inform leadership development across the higher education sector.

A challenge for leadership development

Our stories revealed that sometimes heroic leadership is desired, but only when the relational is built. The consistent micro-moments of knowing our teams, of asking for counsel, of facilitating rather than enforcing change build trust, and this was more important than the persistent invulnerable leader. We recognised that sometimes the heroic leader needs to be performed, but this is just an image to provide temporary stability in moments of extreme instability. Our storytelling then has challenged our perception of the relational and heroic, maybe they are not quite in opposition all of the time, but we also heed Collinson et al.’s (2018) warning of romanticising the notion of heroic leaders. So, maybe the heroic is a temporary tool when crisis emerges?

Ultimately, our stories convinced us that relational leadership must sit at the heart of leadership development. It creates space for empathy, trust and multiple perspectives. While moments of crisis may occasionally call for heroic action, it is the day-to-day relational work of leadership that enables people to contribute and thrive.

We invite readers to consider the same question we asked each other: how have your origin stories shaped your leadership journey so far, and what might your ‘maturing stories’ reveal as you navigate the complexities of leadership in higher education?

Dr Mark Flisher is the Head of the Institute of Arts and Humanities, and Dr Rachael Paige is the interim Head of the Institute of Education, both at the University of Worcester. They are working together on a project exploring relational leadership in higher education and ‘challenging the heroic’.

title: Schüler attackiert: Tritte ins Gesicht: Jugendgewalt schockiert Brandenburg
summary: Mehrere Jugendliche sollen in Frankfurt (Oder) einen Schüler zusammengeschlagen haben. Ein Video dokumentiert den brutalen Angriff. Sozialminister und Oberbürgermeister zeigen sich erschüttert.
full_text:
Tritte gegen das Gesicht, Fausthiebe und filmendes Publikum: Nach Bekanntwerden einer brutalen Attacke von Jugendlichen gegen einen Schüler herrscht in Brandenburg tiefes Entsetzen. „Was einem jungen Menschen hier in Frankfurt (Oder) angetan wurde, macht mich fassungslos“, schrieb Oberbürgermeister Axel Strasser (parteilos) bei Instagram. Es schmerze, solche Gewalt mitansehen zu müssen. „Niemand sollte so etwas durchmachen müssen.“

Aktuell ermittelt die Polizei nach eigenen Angaben gegen zehn Tatverdächtige. Bei ihnen handelt es sich um Kinder und Jugendliche im Alter zwischen 13 und 15 Jahren, die deutscher, polnischer, russischer und syrischer Nationalität sind. Ihnen werden gefährliche Körperverletzung und Raub vorgeworfen.

F.A.Z.-Artikel häufiger in Ihren Suchergebnissen sehen

F.A.Z. bei Google bevorzugen

Brandenburgs Sozialminister und ehemaliges Stadtoberhaupt, René Wilke, drohte mit drastischen Konsequenzen für die Tatverdächtigen. „Wer für Unsicherheit in unserem Land sorgt, kann sich nicht auf die Unsicherheit in seinem Herkunftsland berufen“, schrieb der SPD-Politiker auf Instagram. Er sei bereit, die neuen „Möglichkeiten zur Aberkennung eines Schutzstatus oder zur Aufenthaltsbeendigung konsequent auszuschöpfen“.

Mehrere Jugendliche hatten am Mittwoch in Frankfurt (Oder) vor einer Oberschule auf einen Schüler eingetreten und ihn geschlagen. „Der Junge wies Gesichtsverletzungen auf“, schrieb ein Sprecher der Polizei. Die Schwere der Verletzung ließ er offen.

Video mit entsetzlichen Szenen

Ein Video, das der Polizei vorliegt und das den Angriff zeigen soll, offenbart die Dimension der Gewalt. Zu sehen sind etwa zehn Jugendliche, die einen anderen Jungen zunächst bedrängen, und dann auf ihn einschlagen und treten, auch gegen den Kopf. Auch als ihr wehrloses Opfer zu Boden geht, lassen sie nicht von ihm ab. Die Polizei hält das Video für authentisch. Zunächst hatte die „Märkische Oderzeitung“ berichtet.

Doch was meint Minister Wilke, wenn er nun bleiberechtliche Konsequenzen androht? Es gebe im Aufenthaltsrecht Änderungen, sagte der Minister. Basis sei die Frage, ob etwa Syrien oder Afghanistan sichere Herkunftsländer seien. Daraus könne sich eine Aberkennung des Schutzstatus ergeben. Bei einer Prüfung werde schließlich auch die persönliche Situation des Betroffenen in Betracht gezogen. Wenn „da schon Straftaten und ein Sozialleistungsbezug für einen längeren Zeitraum“ bestünden, wirke sich das nicht positiv aus.

„Man wird sich die Fälle im Detail anschauen müssen“, so Wilke. „Für Jugendliche gilt, dass da auch Urteile ergehen können.“ Diese könnten, wenn die Jugendlichen nicht mehr minderjährig sind, zu Abschiebungen führen. Auch wenn es sich um eine Familie handele, die Rahmenbedingungen aufweise, „die nicht für besondere Integration sprechen und auf dieses Verhalten des Jugendlichen befördernd wirken, dann ist das ein Ausgangspunkt“.

Wilke machte in seinem Post deutlich, wie tief ihn die Aufnahmen von dem Angriff „erschüttert“ hätten. Es mache betroffen und wütend. Die Sicherheitsbehörden würden nun ermitteln. „Niemand schaut weg“, schrieb Wilke. „Alle schauen genau hin. Und das sollten die Täter auch wissen.“ Frankfurts Oberbürgermeister Strasser versprach, er werde sich „dafür einsetzen, dass wir als Stadt gemeinsam mit den zuständigen Stellen die richtigen Konsequenzen ziehen“.

Polizei stellt Tatverdächtige in Schule

Die Polizei reagierte umgehend, nachdem das Opfer den Vorfall gemeldet hatte, und nahm einen Teil der Tatverdächtigen noch während des laufenden Unterrichts fest. Man habe mit „der dringend gebotenen Entschlossenheit“ gehandelt, sagte ein Polizeisprecher. Nach ersten Erkenntnissen zu den Tatverdächtigen habe man sich direkt aufgestellt und die Jugendlichen in deren Schule aufgesucht, um „sie der Strafverfolgung zuzuführen“.

„Wir reden im Moment über einen Einzelfall, der sehr drastisch ist“, sagte ein Sprecher der Stadt Frankfurt (Oder). Die Täter seien ermittelt. Nun folgten Sicherheitsgespräche verschiedener Behörden. Auch die Polizei und die Ausländerbehörde sollen beteiligt sein. Die betroffene Oberschule, vor der der Jugendliche angegriffen wurde, wollte sich auf Anfrage nicht äußern. Auch die Schule, auf die mehrere der mutmaßlichen Täter gehen, wollte kein Statement abgeben.

„Dieses Ausmaß an organisierter Jugendgewalt hatten wir bisher in Frankfurt (Oder) nicht“, sagte Oberbürgermeister Axel Strasser laut einer Mitteilung. Er stehe dazu auch in intensivem Austausch mit dem brandenburgischen Innenminister und der Polizei. Man plane nun, „im Zusammenspiel von Polizei, Staatsanwaltschaft, der Ausländerbehörde, weiteren städtischen Ämtern, Schulen und der Schulsozialarbeit diesen Überfall“ aufzuarbeiten. Das erste Gespräch soll am 27. Oktober stattfinden.

Das Problem der Jugendgewalt ist aktuell in mehreren Brandenburger Städten ein Thema. Der Landtag beschäftigte sich damit in einer Aktuellen Stunde am Mittwoch. In Potsdam sorgten zuletzt mehrere brutale Angriffe für Entsetzen. Seit 2024 wurden laut Innenminister Jan Redmann (CDU) vermehrt migrantisch geprägte Jugendgruppen in Potsdam polizeilich auffällig. In Cottbus kam zuletzt nach Gewaltattacken sogar Sicherheitspersonal an mindestens einer Schule zum Einsatz. Schüler wurden aus Sicherheitsgründen von der Schule genommen.

title: Retos urgentes ante la crisis global
summary:
Conversatorio “Repensar el Trabajo” – 22 de octubre

La entrada Retos urgentes ante la crisis global se publicó primero en CLACSO.
full_text:
El mundo del trabajo atraviesa un proceso de profundas transformaciones. La digitalización, las plataformas y la inteligencia artificial conviven con fenómenos de larga, como la informalidad, la tercerización, las desigualdades y la heterogeneidad de las formas de inserción laboral.

Estas transformaciones interpelan no solo las formas de producir y trabajar, sino también las instituciones construidas históricamente alrededor del empleo: los derechos laborales, la protección social, la regulación y las formas de representación y organización colectiva.

La mesa propone poner en diálogo miradas sindicales, político-institucionales y académicas para pensar estos cambios y discutir qué respuestas necesitamos construir frente a un mundo del trabajo cada vez más heterogéneo. El objetivo es avanzar del diagnóstico hacia una pregunta política: qué nueva agenda de derechos, protección y organización colectiva requiere el trabajo contemporáneo.

El jueves 22 de octubre, a las 14:00 de Argentina (UTC-3), todos estos temas se debatirán en el Conversatorio virtual “Repensar el Trabajo: Retos urgentes ante la crisis global”

Exponen:

Juan Ottaviano (IDAES-UNSAM, Argentina)

Marcelo Di Stefano (Secretario de Fortalecimiento Institucional, Confederación Sindical de trabajadoras y trabajadores de las Américas, CSA, Guatemala)

Jeannette Jara (Universidad de Santiago, Chile)

Marga Ferré (Transform! Europe, España)

Moderan:

Adoración Guamán (Universidad de Valencia, España, co-coordinadora del GT CLACSO ¿Qué trabajo para qué futuro?)

Nora Goren (Universidad Nacional de José C. Paz, Argentina, co-coordinadora del GT CLACSO ¿Qué trabajo para qué futuro?)

Organiza: Grupo de Trabajo de CLACSO “¿Qué trabajo para qué futuro?”

title: The Cost of Knowledge: quando il prezzo lo paga la scienza
summary: Riprendiamo questo post apparso sul sito openscience.unimi.it. A pochi giorni dall’inizio della Open access week 2026 che ha proprio come titolo The cost of Knowledge è lecito interrogarsi non soltanto sul costo economico dell’accesso alla conoscenza, ma anche sul costo che gli attuali sistemi di produzione, valutazione e diffusione della ricerca impongono alla qualità, all’integrità […]
full_text:
Riprendiamo questo post apparso sul sito openscience.unimi.it. A pochi giorni dall’inizio della Open access week 2026 che ha proprio come titolo The cost of Knowledge è lecito interrogarsi non soltanto sul costo economico dell’accesso alla conoscenza, ma anche sul costo che gli attuali sistemi di produzione, valutazione e diffusione della ricerca impongono alla qualità, all’integrità e alla credibilità della scienza stessa

Nel 2012 il matematico e Medaglia Fields Tim Gowers diede avvio a The Cost of Knowledge, una delle più importanti mobilitazioni della comunità accademica contro il sistema dell’editoria scientifica commerciale. La protesta nacque dalla crescente insoddisfazione per l’aumento dei costi degli abbonamenti, per i margini di profitto dei grandi editori e per le restrizioni all’accesso alla conoscenza all’interno di una comunità che da tempo comunicava i propri risultati attraverso gli archivi di pre-print. Migliaia di ricercatori (non solo matematici) aderirono all’iniziativa impegnandosi a non pubblicare, non svolgere attività di revisione e non partecipare agli editorial board di riviste Elsevier.

Tuttavia, la mobilitazione non riuscì a produrre quella trasformazione sistemica che molti auspicavano. Le grandi case editrici scientifiche rappresentano infatti attori economici e politici estremamente influenti, capaci di esercitare un forte potere negoziale nei confronti di università, governi e agenzie di finanziamento. Ma soprattutto, il sistema editoriale continua a essere sostenuto da un elemento strutturale ancora più difficile da scardinare: la valutazione della ricerca. Finché carriere, finanziamenti e reputazione accademica rimarranno legati alla pubblicazione in riviste considerate prestigiose e riconoscibili attraverso determinati marchi, indicatori e classificazioni, i ricercatori continueranno ad alimentare un sistema che oggi come oggi presenta enormi criticità.

In questo senso, The Cost of Knowledge ha mostrato con grande anticipo come la riforma dell’editoria e la riforma della valutazione siano inseparabili. Non è possibile cambiare davvero i modelli di pubblicazione senza mettere in discussione gli incentivi che guidano il comportamento dei ricercatori. È significativo che lo stesso Gowers, anziché limitarsi alla protesta, abbia contribuito a costruire alternative concrete promuovendo Discrete Analysis, una rivista Diamond Open Access che non richiede costi né ai lettori né agli autori, che ha nel suo editorial board due Medaglie Fields e che dimostra come sia possibile organizzare una comunicazione scientifica di elevata qualità senza dipendere dalle logiche commerciali dominanti.

A più di dieci anni di distanza, molte delle criticità denunciate allora non solo non sono state risolte, ma si sono intrecciate con una crisi più ampia della comunicazione scientifica. Il sistema è sempre più condizionato dalla logica del publish or perish, che incentiva la quantità più della qualità e alimenta una crescita incessante del numero di articoli pubblicati. Ogni anno vengono prodotti milioni di lavori, molti dei quali ricevono poca o nessuna attenzione dalla comunità scientifica. Iniziative importanti come Arxiv hanno dovuto cambiare più volte le proprie politiche di accettazione degli articoli perché sommersi da “ricerche” prive di senso.

A questa sovrapproduzione corrisponde una crescente reviewer fatigue. Mentre il numero di manoscritti continua ad aumentare, il numero dei ricercatori resta stabile e il tempo disponibile per valutare le ricerche diminuisce. I revisori sono chiamati a esaminare un numero sempre maggiore di lavori senza che il loro contributo venga adeguatamente riconosciuto. Il risultato è un sistema che fatica sempre più a garantire controlli rigorosi e tempestivi, proprio mentre la massa di risultati da verificare continua a crescere.

La pressione competitiva favorisce inoltre comportamenti opportunistici da parte di alcuni ricercatori: frammentazione artificiale dei risultati, uso strategico delle citazioni, iperautorialità, ricerca orientata a ciò che è rapidamente pubblicabile piuttosto che a ciò che è realmente rilevante. Nei casi più estremi emergono fenomeni come paper mills, manipolazione delle revisioni e frodi. Non si tratta soltanto di problemi individuali, ma di conseguenze prevedibili di un sistema che premia indicatori quantitativi e produttività apparente.

In questo contesto, i contratti trasformativi sono stati presentati come uno strumento per accompagnare il passaggio dagli abbonamenti tradizionali all’Open Access, convertendo la spesa per leggere in spesa per pubblicare. Tuttavia, le analisi condotte nel Regno Unito da Jisc e le valutazioni di cOAlition S mostrano un quadro ambiguo: gli accordi hanno favorito la crescita delle pubblicazioni ad accesso aperto e la conformità alle policy dei finanziatori, ma non hanno prodotto la trasformazione strutturale attesa. Molti grandi editori continuano infatti a basare il proprio modello economico su logiche ereditate dall’era degli abbonamenti (aumento dei costi sempre e comunque), mentre accordi concepiti come temporanei rischiano di diventare una componente permanente (e insostenibile) del sistema.

Parallelamente, negli ultimi anni si è assistito a un fenomeno sempre più significativo: le dimissioni collettive degli editorial board. Dai casi pionieristici di Lingua fino alle numerose dimissioni registrate più recentemente, ricercatori ed editor denunciano una crescente incompatibilità tra gli interessi della comunità scientifica e quelli di operatori commerciali orientati alla crescita continua dei volumi pubblicati e dei ricavi generati. In molti casi, gli editorial board hanno lasciato le riviste storiche per fondarne di nuove, spesso Diamond Open Access e governate direttamente dalle comunità disciplinari.

Questi eventi non rappresentano episodi isolati. Segnalano piuttosto una crescente consapevolezza che il costo non riguarda soltanto l’accesso alla conoscenza, ma il modo stesso in cui la conoscenza viene prodotta, valutata, pubblicata e utilizzata. La questione centrale non è più soltanto chi paga per leggere o per pubblicare, ma chi controlla le infrastrutture della comunicazione scientifica, chi governa i processi editoriali e quali valori debbano orientare la diffusione della ricerca.

È in questo scenario che prende forma la visione di una New Publication Culture, sostenuta dalle università Olandesi. Una cultura in cui la pubblicazione non è più identificata con il prestigio di una rivista commerciale o con indicatori bibliometrici prodotti da soggetti privati, ma con la qualità, la trasparenza, la riproducibilità e la riusabilità della ricerca. Una cultura che valorizza la peer review come bene comune, promuove infrastrutture aperte e governate dalle comunità accademiche, sostiene i modelli Diamond Open Access e si integra con i principi della valutazione responsabile della ricerca.

Se The Cost of Knowledge ha rappresentato la denuncia dei problemi del sistema, la crisi dell’attuale sistema editoriale mostra che la posta in gioco è oggi ancora più alta. Il vero punto in discussione non è più ormai ridurre i costi della conoscenza o rendere aperti gli articoli, ma ripensare gli incentivi che guidano la produzione scientifica e costruire un sistema capace di generare meno rumore e più conoscenza affidabile. In altre parole, passare da una riforma dei meccanismi di pagamento in cui gli interlocutori sono soggetti privati a una vera trasformazione della cultura della comunicazione scientifica.

Il tema della Open Access Week 2026, The Cost of Knowledge, richiama la celebre iniziativa lanciata da Timothy Gowers nel 2012 contro le distorsioni dell’editoria scientifica commerciale. A quasi quindici anni di distanza, il richiamo a quel dibattito offre l’occasione per una riflessione più ampia sul percorso compiuto dall’Open Access e, più in generale, dalla ricerca scientifica.

Oggi più che mai è importante evitare che la discussione si riduca a una questione di modelli di business, di tariffe APC, di accordi trasformativi o di dettagli contrattuali. Sono temi rilevanti, ma rischiano di farci perdere di vista la domanda fondamentale: il sistema della comunicazione scientifica sta realmente aiutando la ricerca a produrre e diffondere conoscenza migliore, più affidabile e più utile alla società?

Negli ultimi quindici anni l’accesso alla letteratura scientifica è indubbiamente aumentato, ma nello stesso periodo sono emerse nuove criticità, per questo motivo, parlare oggi di The Cost of Knowledge significa interrogarsi non soltanto sul costo economico dell’accesso alla conoscenza, ma anche sul costo che gli attuali sistemi di produzione, valutazione e diffusione della ricerca impongono alla qualità, all’integrità e alla credibilità della scienza stessa.

La sfida, dunque, non è semplicemente rendere aperti gli articoli, ma costruire un sistema che metta nuovamente la ricerca al centro, evitando che metriche, modelli di business e procedure amministrative diventino un fine anziché uno strumento. In altre parole, il vero tema non è il costo dell’accesso alla conoscenza, ma il costo che siamo disposti a pagare quando perdiamo di vista la conoscenza stessa.

Finché carriere, finanziamenti e reputazione accademica rimarranno legati alla pubblicazione in riviste considerate prestigiose e riconoscibili attraverso determinati marchi, indicatori e classificazioni, i ricercatori continueranno ad alimentare un sistema che oggi come oggi presenta enormi criticità.

In questo senso, The Cost of Knowledge ha mostrato con grande anticipo come la riforma dell’editoria e la riforma della valutazione siano inseparabili. Non è possibile cambiare davvero i modelli di pubblicazione senza mettere in discussione gli incentivi che guidano il comportamento dei ricercatori. È significativo che lo stesso Gowers, anziché limitarsi alla protesta, abbia contribuito a costruire alternative concrete promuovendo Discrete Analysis, una rivista Diamond Open Access che non richiede costi né ai lettori né agli autori, che ha nel suo editorial board due Medaglie Fields e che dimostra come sia possibile organizzare una comunicazione scientifica di elevata qualità senza dipendere dalle logiche commerciali dominanti.

A più di dieci anni di distanza, molte delle criticità denunciate allora non solo non sono state risolte, ma si sono intrecciate con una crisi più ampia della comunicazione scientifica. Il sistema è sempre più condizionato dalla logica del publish or perish, che incentiva la quantità più della qualità e alimenta una crescita incessante del numero di articoli pubblicati. Ogni anno vengono prodotti milioni di lavori, molti dei quali ricevono poca o nessuna attenzione dalla comunità scientifica. Iniziative importanti come Arxiv hanno dovuto cambiare più volte le proprie politiche di accettazione degli articoli perché sommersi da “ricerche” prive di senso.

A questa sovrapproduzione corrisponde una crescente reviewer fatigue. Mentre il numero di manoscritti continua ad aumentare, il numero dei ricercatori resta stabile e il tempo disponibile per valutare le ricerche diminuisce. I revisori sono chiamati a esaminare un numero sempre maggiore di lavori senza che il loro contributo venga adeguatamente riconosciuto. Il risultato è un sistema che fatica sempre più a garantire controlli rigorosi e tempestivi, proprio mentre la massa di risultati da verificare continua a crescere.

La pressione competitiva favorisce inoltre comportamenti opportunistici da parte di alcuni ricercatori: frammentazione artificiale dei risultati, uso strategico delle citazioni, iperautorialità, ricerca orientata a ciò che è rapidamente pubblicabile piuttosto che a ciò che è realmente rilevante. Nei casi più estremi emergono fenomeni come paper mills, manipolazione delle revisioni e frodi. Non si tratta soltanto di problemi individuali, ma di conseguenze prevedibili di un sistema che premia indicatori quantitativi e produttività apparente.

In questo contesto, i contratti trasformativi sono stati presentati come uno strumento per accompagnare il passaggio dagli abbonamenti tradizionali all’Open Access, convertendo la spesa per leggere in spesa per pubblicare. Tuttavia, le analisi condotte nel Regno Unito da Jisc e le valutazioni di cOAlition S mostrano un quadro ambiguo: gli accordi hanno favorito la crescita delle pubblicazioni ad accesso aperto e la conformità alle policy dei finanziatori, ma non hanno prodotto la trasformazione strutturale attesa. Molti grandi editori continuano infatti a basare il proprio modello economico su logiche ereditate dall’era degli abbonamenti (aumento dei costi sempre e comunque), mentre accordi concepiti come temporanei rischiano di diventare una componente permanente (e insostenibile) del sistema.

Parallelamente, negli ultimi anni si è assistito a un fenomeno sempre più significativo: le dimissioni collettive degli editorial board. Dai casi pionieristici di Lingua fino alle numerose dimissioni registrate più recentemente, ricercatori ed editor denunciano una crescente incompatibilità tra gli interessi della comunità scientifica e quelli di operatori commerciali orientati alla crescita continua dei volumi pubblicati e dei ricavi generati. In molti casi, gli editorial board hanno lasciato le riviste storiche per fondarne di nuove, spesso Diamond Open Access e governate direttamente dalle comunità disciplinari.

Questi eventi non rappresentano episodi isolati. Segnalano piuttosto una crescente consapevolezza che il costo non riguarda soltanto l’accesso alla conoscenza, ma il modo stesso in cui la conoscenza viene prodotta, valutata, pubblicata e utilizzata. La questione centrale non è più soltanto chi paga per leggere o per pubblicare, ma chi controlla le infrastrutture della comunicazione scientifica, chi governa i processi editoriali e quali valori debbano orientare la diffusione della ricerca.

È in questo scenario che prende forma la visione di una New Publication Culture, sostenuta dalle università Olandesi. Una cultura in cui la pubblicazione non è più identificata con il prestigio di una rivista commerciale o con indicatori bibliometrici prodotti da soggetti privati, ma con la qualità, la trasparenza, la riproducibilità e la riusabilità della ricerca. Una cultura che valorizza la peer review come bene comune, promuove infrastrutture aperte e governate dalle comunità accademiche, sostiene i modelli Diamond Open Access e si integra con i principi della valutazione responsabile della ricerca.

Se The Cost of Knowledge ha rappresentato la denuncia dei problemi del sistema, la crisi dell’attuale sistema editoriale mostra che la posta in gioco è oggi ancora più alta. Il vero punto in discussione non è più ormai ridurre i costi della conoscenza o rendere aperti gli articoli, ma ripensare gli incentivi che guidano la produzione scientifica e costruire un sistema capace di generare meno rumore e più conoscenza affidabile. In altre parole, passare da una riforma dei meccanismi di pagamento in cui gli interlocutori sono soggetti privati a una vera trasformazione della cultura della comunicazione scientifica.

Il tema della Open Access Week 2026, The Cost of Knowledge, richiama la celebre iniziativa lanciata da Timothy Gowers nel 2012 contro le distorsioni dell’editoria scientifica commerciale. A quasi quindici anni di distanza, il richiamo a quel dibattito offre l’occasione per una riflessione più ampia sul percorso compiuto dall’Open Access e, più in generale, dalla ricerca scientifica.

Oggi più che mai è importante evitare che la discussione si riduca a una questione di modelli di business, di tariffe APC, di accordi trasformativi o di dettagli contrattuali. Sono temi rilevanti, ma rischiano di farci perdere di vista la domanda fondamentale: il sistema della comunicazione scientifica sta realmente aiutando la ricerca a produrre e diffondere conoscenza migliore, più affidabile e più utile alla società?

Negli ultimi quindici anni l’accesso alla letteratura scientifica è indubbiamente aumentato, ma nello stesso periodo sono emerse nuove criticità, per questo motivo, parlare oggi di The Cost of Knowledge significa interrogarsi non soltanto sul costo economico dell’accesso alla conoscenza, ma anche sul costo che gli attuali sistemi di produzione, valutazione e diffusione della ricerca impongono alla qualità, all’integrità e alla credibilità della scienza stessa.

La sfida, dunque, non è semplicemente rendere aperti gli articoli, ma costruire un sistema che metta nuovamente la ricerca al centro, evitando che metriche, modelli di business e procedure amministrative diventino un fine anziché uno strumento. In altre parole, il vero tema non è il costo dell’accesso alla conoscenza, ma il costo che siamo disposti a pagare quando perdiamo di vista la conoscenza stessa.
